title: Cost levers
summary: Six levers cut spend: trim the prompt, cache the stable prefix, cap output, choose a cheaper model, move work to batch tiers, and reuse whole answers. Each has a break-even and a catch.
useIf: You know which token sink dominates and must pick the lever that fits it.
avoidIf: You have not attributed spend yet, or you would trade answer quality you have not measured.

explain.md: Pull levers in the order of **sink size, effort and risk**. Output tokens are the costliest class, and OpenAI's rule of thumb is that halving output tokens may cut about half the latency while halving the prompt may cut only 1% to 5% [[tr8]]. Input trimming still saves money in proportion to tokens, so latency and cost do not rank levers the same way.

**Prompt caching** reads a repeated prefix at 0.1x but writes it at 1.25x on GPT-5.6 and later, so it breaks even at the second request inside the lifetime: 1.25 + 0.1(N-1) against N [[r25]]. Anthropic's 1-hour entry writes at 2x and needs three requests (2.2x against 3x) [[r26]]. A **semantic cache** skips the whole call on a hit but pays an embedding and a vector lookup on every miss, and Microsoft warns hits can be incorrect, outdated or unsafe [[tr1]]. **Batch** and **Flex** halve the price in return for time [[r12]] [[r11]].

pitfalls.symptom: Cache hit ratio is near zero after a release
pitfalls.cause: A timestamp, reordered tools or a changed effort setting moved the prefix
pitfalls.fix: Put static content first, keep tool order stable, alert on cached tokens over prompt tokens

pitfalls.symptom: A semantic cache returns another user's answer
pitfalls.cause: The cache key ignores tenant, user, model or prompt version
pitfalls.fix: Partition with `vary-by` and include model, embedding model, template and policy versions in the key [[tr2]]

pitfalls.cause: Low repeat rate, so most requests pay embedding plus lookup plus the normal call
pitfalls.fix: Measure net savings per miss and hit; drop the cache if hits stay low

scenarios.title: A fat, stable prefix in an agent loop
scenarios.situation: A tool-using agent makes 8 to 15 calls per task. Each call carries 12,000 tokens of tool definitions and system text plus a growing history.
constraints: The tool set is stable inside a session
Traffic is steady through the day
unknowns: Is the prefix byte-identical across calls?
How often do sessions go idle longer than the lifetime?
Is the deployment PTU-M, which has no breakpoints?
scenarios.question: Which change saves the most first?

options.name: Order tools and system first, keep history append-only, remove early timestamps
options.why: Calls after the first read the 12,000 tokens at a tenth of the price and with lower time to first token.
options.tradeoff: Any tool change or compaction resets reuse, and each first write costs 1.25x.

options.name: Trim tool results and compact old history
options.why: Shrinks the growing part of the prompt.
options.tradeoff: Compaction rewrites the prefix and resets the cache.

options.name: Move every step to the smallest model
options.why: Weaker planning can add steps, which multiplies the re-sent prefix.
options.tradeoff: Fine for narrow sub-steps behind a router once evals pass.

flips.if: Sessions rarely make a second call inside the lifetime
flips.then: Caching saves little; shrink the tool list instead.

flips.if: Gaps between calls run 5 to 60 minutes on Anthropic
flips.then: The 1-hour TTL can pay, but only from the third request.

scenarios.takeaway: In loops the repeated prefix is the bill. Make it cacheable first.

scenarios.title: Nightly enrichment of two million records
scenarios.situation: A pipeline classifies and summarises records overnight. Results are read the next morning. Volume is large and the model is fixed.
unknowns: Does the model support the batch tier?
Is enqueued-token quota enough for one night's input?
scenarios.question: Where does the work run?

options.name: Batch tier with a 24-hour target
options.why: Half price on Azure, OpenAI and Anthropic, with separate quota that does not touch interactive traffic.
options.tradeoff: No real-time SLA, so the eight-hour window is a risk if jobs queue longer; split jobs and monitor.

options.name: Flex processing
options.why: Also 50% off with a synchronous API shape.
options.tradeoff: Preview on Azure, preemptible: expect 429 and 408 and build your own retry. It shares quota with Standard.

options.name: Provisioned throughput for the nightly peak
options.why: PTUs bill every hour whether or not requests arrive, so a nightly job pays for idle days.

flips.if: Results must be ready within 30 minutes
flips.then: Batch is too slow; use Flex with fallback or Standard.

flips.if: The model has no batch support
flips.then: Use Standard with a client-side rate limiter and off-peak scheduling.

scenarios.takeaway: If nobody waits, do not pay for waiting.

scenarios.title: A public FAQ assistant
scenarios.situation: A public assistant answers product questions from one shared knowledge base. About 40% of questions are paraphrases of the same few hundred. No user data is involved.
constraints: Content is identical for every caller
A wrong answer is a minor support cost
Answers change when the knowledge base is republished
unknowns: What is the measured paraphrase rate?
How strict can the similarity threshold be?
How is the cache invalidated on republish?
scenarios.question: Is a semantic cache worth it?

options.name: Yes: gateway semantic cache, strict threshold, TTL, flush on republish
options.why: Content is shared and low risk, so a hit saves the whole call. Start near 0.05 on the APIM scale and add the model and prompt version to the partition.
options.tradeoff: Every miss pays embedding plus lookup; wrong hits are possible.

options.name: Exact-match response cache only
options.why: No similarity risk and simple invalidation.
options.tradeoff: Misses paraphrases, so hit rate is lower.

options.name: No cache; rely on prompt caching
options.why: It leaves 40% repeat traffic paying full output cost.
options.tradeoff: Right when answers are permissioned or the repeat rate is low.

flips.if: Answers depend on the caller's entitlements
flips.then: Partition by identity scope or skip semantic caching.
Net savings are small; skip it.

scenarios.takeaway: Semantic caching pays for shared, low-risk, repetitive content only.

quiz.q: An Anthropic 1-hour cache entry writes at 2x and reads at 0.1x. What is the smallest number of requests inside the hour for which caching costs less than uncached?
quiz.explain: Cost is 2 + 0.1(N-1) against N. N=2 gives 2.1 against 2, which loses. N=3 gives 2.2 against 3, which wins [[r26]].

quiz.q: You deploy an APIM semantic cache for the first time. Which `score-threshold` is the safest start?
options: About 0.05, then tune with measured wrong-hit rates
quiz.explain: In APIM a lower score is stricter. Microsoft suggests starting low and warns that above 0.2 may mismatch [[tr1]]. Higher values add hits and wrong answers; 0.8 would match loosely.

quiz.q: Match each lever to its main catch.

pairs.r: Silent misses when the prefix drifts

quiz.explain: Each lever fails differently. The prompt cache keeps the model output unchanged but needs monitoring; a semantic cache changes what users see.

flashcards.front: When does a 1.25x write plus 0.1x reads beat uncached?
flashcards.back: From the second request inside the lifetime: 1.25 + 0.1(N-1) against N. One use loses 25%.

flashcards.front: Which saves more latency: halving output or halving input?
flashcards.back: Output, roughly half the latency by OpenAI's rule of thumb. Halving input may save only 1% to 5% of latency, though it still cuts cost.

flashcards.front: What does a semantic cache cost on a miss?
flashcards.back: An embedding call plus a vector lookup before the normal model call. Net savings need a high hit rate.
